megillah-3a-4-5.note: When Yonatan ben Uzziel wrote his Aramaic translation of the Prophets, the land of Israel quaked and a Divine Voice asked who had revealed God's secrets to mankind. Yonatan stood up and said it was he, and that he had done it not for his own honor or his family's, but for God's honor, so that disputes would not multiply among the Jewish people. He also wanted to translate the Writings, but a Divine Voice told him: 'It is enough for you.' The Gemara explains that the Writings contain the time of the Messiah's coming.
megillah-3a-4-5.why: The Gemara has just reported who composed the Aramaic translations read in synagogues, Onkelos for the Torah and Yonatan ben Uzziel for the Prophets. This account continues the report of Yonatan's work, and the Gemara then asks why his translation shook the land when Onkelos's did not.

people.name: Yonatan ben Uzziel
people.about: The author of the Aramaic translation of the Prophets, who answers the Divine Voice.

people.name: God
people.about: Speaks through a Divine Voice, challenging Yonatan and then stopping him from translating the Writings.

terms.meaning: A voice from heaven that announces God's will.
The third part of the Hebrew Bible, after the Torah and the Prophets; it includes Psalms, Proverbs, Esther and Daniel.
Here, an Aramaic rendering of the Bible, read aloud in synagogues so people could understand the Hebrew text.

megillah-5a-18-18.note: Rabbi Elazar reported in the name of Rabbi Hanina that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi planted a sapling on Purim, bathed in Tzippori on the seventeenth of Tammuz when the market wagons were passing, and sought to abolish the fast of the Ninth of Av, and that the Sages did not agree with him. Rabbi Abba bar Zavda said to Rabbi Elazar that it had not happened that way. That year, he said, the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat and was postponed to Sunday, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said that since it had been pushed off, it should be pushed off altogether; the Rabbis did not agree with him. Rabbi Elazar applied to him the verse 'Two are better than one.'
megillah-5a-18-18.why: The Gemara goes on to ask how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi could plant on Purim, when work is forbidden then, and answers that he planted on the day that was not Purim where he lived. The planting raises the question of which towns keep Purim on the fourteenth and which on the fifteenth.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; the Sage whose unusual acts on Purim, the seventeenth of Tammuz and the Ninth of Av are reported.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Reports the incidents in the name of Rabbi Hanina.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: The Sage in whose name Rabbi Elazar reports the incidents.

people.name: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda
people.about: Corrects Rabbi Elazar's account of what Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said about the Ninth of Av.

terms.meaning: A summer fast day marking the breach of Jerusalem's walls, three weeks before the Ninth of Av.
The fast day mourning the destruction of the Temples.
The holiday celebrating the rescue of the Jews in the book of Esther, kept on the fourteenth or fifteenth of Adar depending on the town.

megillah-7a-20-20.note: On Purim, Rabbi Yehuda Nesia sent Rabbi Oshaya the leg of a calf and a jug of wine. Rabbi Oshaya sent back his thanks: 'You have fulfilled through us, our teacher, both sending portions one to another and gifts to the poor.'
megillah-7a-20-20.why: Rav Yosef has just taught that the verse in Esther requires two portions to one person and gifts to the poor. Rabbi Oshaya's reply shows a single generous gift to a poor scholar counting for both mitzvot.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: Sent a Purim gift of meat and wine to Rabbi Oshaya.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: Received the gift; the text says he was poor, so it counted as a gift to the poor as well.

terms.meaning: The Purim mitzva, from the book of Esther, of sending gifts of food to a friend.
The Purim mitzva of giving charity to poor people.
A calf of especially fine quality, here a choice cut of meat.

megillah-7b-1-3.note: Rabba sent Marei bar Mar a Purim gift by the hand of Abaye: a sack of dates and a cup of roasted flour. Abaye said Marei would now quote the saying, 'Even if a farmer becomes king, the basket does not leave his neck.' Marei bar Mar sent back a sack of ginger and a cup of long peppers, and Abaye said Rabba would now say, 'I sent him sweet things and he sent me sharp ones.' Abaye later said that he left Rabba's house already full, but at Marei bar Mar's he was served sixty plates of sixty dishes, ate sixty portions, and still wanted to eat the plate after the last one, a pot roast.
megillah-7b-1-3.why: The Gemara is discussing the Purim mitzva of sending portions of food to a friend; this exchange follows the gift of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia to Rabbi Oshaya as another example, and Abaye then draws two folk sayings from his meal.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Sent a plain Purim gift to Marei bar Mar; the translation's note says he was poor.

people.name: Marei bar Mar
people.about: Received Rabba's gift and sent back a costlier one, then hosted Abaye lavishly.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rabba's nephew and student, who carried the gifts and comments on each one.

terms.meaning: Gifts of food sent to a friend on Purim, a mitzva from the book of Esther.

megillah-7b-7-7.note: Rabba and Rabbi Zeira held a Purim feast together and became drunk. Rabba arose and slaughtered Rabbi Zeira. The next day Rabba prayed for mercy and brought him back to life. The following year Rabba invited him to hold the Purim feast together again, and Rabbi Zeira answered: 'Miracles do not happen every hour.'
megillah-7b-7-7.why: Rava has just ruled that a person must drink on Purim until he cannot tell 'cursed is Haman' from 'blessed is Mordecai.' This story comes right after that ruling and shows how such drinking once ended.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Held a Purim feast with Rabbi Zeira, killed him while drunk, and revived him through prayer.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Rabba's companion at the feast, who declined to come back the next year.

terms.meaning: The festive meal eaten on Purim day, one of the holiday's mitzvot.

megillah-9a-10-15.note: King Ptolemy gathered seventy-two Elders, put each in a separate room without telling them why, and asked each to write him a translation of the Torah of Moses. God put wisdom in each one's heart, and all of them made the same changes to the text. They wrote, for example, 'God created in the beginning' rather than an order that could read as 'Bereshit created God,' and 'I shall make man' rather than 'Let us make man,' to avoid implying more than one power. They also changed verses that might shame Jacob's sons or Moses. For the hare they wrote 'the short-legged beast,' because Ptolemy's wife was named Arnevet, the Hebrew word for hare, and they did not want him to say the Jews had mocked him by putting her name in the Torah.
megillah-9a-10-15.why: The discussion is about which languages a Torah scroll may be written in; Rabbi Yehuda says the Sages allowed Greek only for a Torah scroll. The Gemara gives the Ptolemy incident as the reason Greek was singled out.

people.name: King Ptolemy
people.about: King of Egypt, who had seventy-two Elders translate the Torah separately.

people.name: God
people.about: Put the same understanding in the heart of each Elder, so all their translations matched.

people.name: the seventy-two Elders
people.about: Sages of Israel who each translated the Torah alone and all made the same changes.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara as an authoritative source.
The Five Books of Moses, the first part of the Hebrew Bible.

megillah-9b-11-11.note: A High Priest became temporarily disqualified, and the priest Rabbi Yosef ben Elem of Tzippori was appointed to serve in his place. When the disqualification passed, the case came before the Sages. They ruled that the original High Priest returns to his service, and the second is fit to serve neither as High Priest nor as an ordinary priest.
megillah-9b-11-11.why: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei disagree about a substitute High Priest once the original returns; Rabbi Yosei cites this case to back his view that the substitute may serve in neither role, and the Gemara gives the reasons: jealousy, and the rule that holiness is raised, never lowered.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yosef ben Elem of Tzippori
people.about: A priest appointed to stand in for a disqualified High Priest.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple, who alone performed certain services.
A temporary condition, such as ritual impurity, that kept the High Priest from serving.
An ordinary priest, below the High Priest.

megillah-14a-0-1.note: Rabbi Abba compares Ahasuerus and Haman to two men: one had a mound of earth in the middle of his field, the other a ditch in his. The owner of the ditch wished he could buy the mound, and the owner of the mound wished he could buy the ditch. One day they met, and the ditch owner said, 'Sell me your mound.' The mound owner answered, 'Take it for free, and gladly.'
megillah-14a-0-1.why: The Gemara is reading Esther verse by verse. Haman has offered the king ten thousand talents of silver, and the king answers, 'The silver is given to you, the people also.' Rabbi Abba's parable explains why the king took no money: he wanted the Jews destroyed just as much as Haman did.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The Sage who tells the parable.

people.name: Ahasuerus
people.about: The Persian king of the book of Esther, compared to one of the two field owners.

people.name: Haman
people.about: The king's minister who wanted to destroy the Jews, compared to the other field owner.

terms.meaning: A short made-up story used to explain something by comparison.

megillah-18a-24-28.note: The Sages did not know what several rare words meant, and learned them from everyday speech. They heard the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house ask Sages coming in a few at a time, 'How long will you come in seirugin seirugin?', and learned that seirugin means at intervals. They heard her use other words while talking to a man scattering purslane, to a man twirling his hair, and to a friend she told to sweep the house, and so learned the words for purslane, for turning something round, and for a broom. Rabba bar bar Hana told how an Arab he was traveling with said to him, 'Take your yehav and throw it on my camel,' and he understood that yehav means a load.
megillah-18a-24-28.why: The mishna rules that one who reads the Megilla seirugin has fulfilled his obligation, and the Gemara needs to know what the word means. The maidservant's question explains it, and the other words follow as a chain of similar cases.

people.name: the maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house
people.about: Her everyday Hebrew taught the Sages the meaning of several rare words.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; the Sage whose household servant is overheard.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Learned the meaning of yehav from an Arab traveling companion.

terms.meaning: The scroll of the book of Esther, read aloud on Purim.
A leafy green plant that grows wild and is eaten as a vegetable.

megillah-18b-12-12.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar told of Rabbi Meir, who went to Asia Minor to fix the calendar by adding a month to the year. When Purim came there was no Megilla there, so he wrote one from memory and read from it.
megillah-18b-12-12.why: Rabbi Yohanan has ruled that one may not write even a single letter of the Bible except by copying from a written text. The Gemara raises Rabbi Meir's Megilla as an objection, and answers that Rabbi Meir knew the text exactly and that an emergency is different.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: Reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who wrote out a Megilla from memory when none could be found.

terms.meaning: The scroll of the book of Esther, read aloud on Purim.
To add an extra month to the Hebrew year to keep the calendar in step with the seasons, a decision made by the Sages.

megillah-22a-18-18.note: Rav came to Babylonia on a public fast day and stood up to read from the Torah scroll. He said a blessing before he began reading, but none when he finished. Afterward everyone else fell on their faces in prayer, but Rav did not fall on his face.
megillah-22a-18-18.why: The Gemara wants to know how many people read from the Torah on a public fast, three or four. It argues from Rav's missing closing blessing that someone read after him, which would make four, and then rejects the proof.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A leading Sage who read from the Torah on a fast day in Babylonia.

terms.meaning: A fast day declared for the whole community, for example in a drought.
Bowing down to the ground during a supplication prayer said after the main prayer.

megillah-22b-9-9.note: Rav came to Babylonia on a public fast day and stood up to read from the Torah scroll. He said a blessing before he began reading, but none when he finished. Everyone else then fell on their faces in prayer, but Rav did not, and the Gemara asks why.
megillah-22b-9-9.why: Having used this incident to count the Torah readers on a fast day, the Gemara now asks why Rav did not bow. It answers that the floor in front of him was stone, and the Torah forbids bowing on figured stone outside the Temple.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A leading Sage who read from the Torah on a fast day in Babylonia and did not bow with the rest.

terms.meaning: A fast day declared for the whole community, for example in a drought.
Bowing down to the ground during a supplication prayer said after the main prayer.

megillah-22b-16-16.note: Levi demonstrated the bow called kidda in front of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and in doing it he became lame.
megillah-22b-16-16.why: The Gemara has just defined three kinds of bowing, kidda among them. It then asks whether this caused Levi's limp, since Rabbi Elazar says Levi was lamed for speaking impertinently to God, and answers that both did.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who became lame while demonstrating a bow.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; the Sage before whom Levi demonstrated the bow.

terms.meaning: A form of bowing with the face toward the ground; the translation's note describes the High Priest's version as bending from the waist until the head touches the ground.

megillah-24b-5-6.note: Rabbi Yosei said that all his life he was troubled by the verse 'You shall grope at noon as the blind man gropes in the darkness': what difference does dark or light make to a blind man? Then one night, walking in total darkness, he met a blind man carrying a torch. He asked, 'My son, why do you need this torch?' The blind man answered: 'As long as I have a torch in my hand, people see me and save me from the pits and the thorns and the thistles.'
megillah-24b-5-6.why: Rabbi Yehuda says a man who has never seen may not say the blessing over the heavenly lights, since he gets no benefit from them. The Rabbis disagree, and this story supplies their reason: a blind man benefits from light too.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage puzzled by a verse until he met a blind man carrying a torch.

people.name: the blind man
people.about: Walking at night with a torch so that others could see him and keep him from harm.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara as an authoritative source.

megillah-25a-4-4.note: A man led the prayers in front of Rabba and said: 'You had pity on the bird's nest, have pity and mercy on us; You had pity on an animal and its young, have pity and mercy on us.' Rabba said, 'How well this rabbi knows how to win his Master's favor!' Abaye said to him: 'But didn't we learn in the mishna that we silence him?'
megillah-25a-4-4.why: The mishna says a prayer leader who mentions God's mercy on the bird's nest is silenced, and two Sages have just given reasons. The Gemara then explains that Rabba knew the rule and spoke only to sharpen Abaye's mind.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who praised the prayer leader's words.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objects to Rabba that the mishna says such a prayer leader is silenced.

terms.meaning: The Torah's command to send away a mother bird before taking her eggs or chicks.
The Torah's ban on slaughtering an animal and its young on the same day.
The early collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.

megillah-25a-6-7.note: A man leading the prayers in front of Rabbi Ḥanina stretched out the opening praise of God, calling Him the great, the mighty, the awesome, the powerful, the strong and the fearless. Rabbi Ḥanina asked him whether he had now finished all the praises of his Master. Even the three standard words, he said, we would not dare to say had Moses not written them in the Torah and the Great Assembly not placed them in the prayer. Piling on more is like praising a man who owns countless thousands of gold coins for owning a thousand silver ones: it insults him.
megillah-25a-6-7.why: The mishna rules that a prayer leader who adds improper wording is silenced, and just before this a leader in front of Rabba added pleas to God's mercy. This is a second case of a leader who added his own words to the fixed prayer.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: The Sage in whose presence the man led the prayers, and who rebuked him for adding praises.

terms.meaning: Led the congregation in prayer; the prayer leader stood in front of the ark holding the Torah scrolls.
The central prayer of every service, said standing, which opens with praises of God.
The body of Sages that, by tradition, fixed the wording of the prayers.
A coin; gold dinars were worth far more than silver ones.

megillah-25b-8-8.note: A man was reading the prophetic portion in the synagogue in front of Rabbi Eliezer, and he read Ezekiel's chapter that opens: Make known to Jerusalem her abominations. Rabbi Eliezer said to him: before you examine the abominations of Jerusalem, go and examine the abominations of your own mother. They looked into the man's lineage and found a stain of illegitimacy in it.
megillah-25b-8-8.why: The Gemara is going through a list of sensitive Bible passages and whether each may be read and translated aloud in synagogue. The list allows this chapter of Ezekiel, and the story shows that Rabbi Eliezer held otherwise, the view the list sets aside.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who objected when a man read Ezekiel's rebuke of Jerusalem in his presence.

terms.meaning: A collection of early teachings from the time of the Mishna, often expanding on it.
A reading from the Prophets that follows the Torah reading in synagogue.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
A flaw in a person's family line, here because his mother had a forbidden sexual relationship.

megillah-25b-9-9.note: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel came to the village of Kavul, where the synagogue sexton was reading aloud the verse telling how Reuben lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, while a translator rendered the reading for the congregation. Rabbi Ḥanina told the translator to stop and translate only the end of the verse. The Sages praised him for it.
megillah-25b-9-9.why: The Gemara is listing passages that are read aloud in synagogue but not translated for the listeners, and the story of Reuben comes first on that list. Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel's instruction shows the rule being applied.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel
people.about: A Sage visiting Kavul who stopped the translator from translating the verse about Reuben.

people.name: Reuben
people.about: Son of Jacob, the subject of the verse being read.

people.name: Bilhah
people.about: His father's concubine, named in the verse.

terms.meaning: In the synagogue each verse of the Torah was read in Hebrew and then translated aloud into the language the people spoke.
The synagogue attendant, here the one reading from the Torah.
A collection of early teachings from the time of the Mishna, often expanding on it.

megillah-26a-7-7.note: Rabbi Yehuda reported that the bronze workers in Jerusalem had a synagogue of their own, which they sold to Rabbi Eliezer, and he used it for all his own needs. The Gemara asks how they could sell it, since Jerusalem is a city, and answers that it was a small synagogue that the bronze workers had built themselves.
megillah-26a-7-7.why: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani, citing Rabbi Yonatan, has just ruled that a village synagogue may be sold but a city synagogue may not, because people from outside use it. This sale in Jerusalem is raised as an objection to that ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who bought the bronze workers' synagogue and used it for his own needs.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
The Gemara cites an earlier source that seems to contradict a ruling just given.

megillah-26b-12-12.note: A synagogue of the Jews of Rome opened onto a room where a corpse was lying, so the impurity of the dead spread into the synagogue, and the priests, who must avoid that impurity, could not go in to pray. They came to Rava, who told them to lift the ark and set it down in the opening between the rooms: a wooden utensil made to stay in one place cannot become impure, so it blocks the impurity. The Rabbis objected that the ark is sometimes moved with a Torah scroll still inside it, which makes it an ordinary movable utensil. Rava answered that if so, there is no remedy.
megillah-26b-12-12.why: The Gemara is collecting Rava's rulings about the ark, its curtain and the cases that hold Torah scrolls; this case adds one more ruling of his about the ark, this time about its legal status as a wooden utensil.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage the priests consult; he proposes using the ark as a barrier, then concedes the objection.

terms.meaning: A dead body imparts the most severe form of ritual impurity, which spreads through a roofed space. Priests are forbidden to contract it.
The cabinet in a synagogue where the Torah scrolls are kept.

terms.term: a wooden utensil designated to rest
terms.meaning: In the purity laws, a large wooden object made to stay in place rather than be carried about cannot become impure, and so can act as a barrier against impurity.

megillah-27a-23-25.note: Rav Huna once decreed a fast day. Rav Hana bar Hanilai and all the people of his town came to Rav Huna, and charity was imposed on them, which they gave. When they were about to go home, they asked Rav Huna to give the money back so they could support the poor of their own town with it. Rav Huna refused, citing a teaching that where a town has a scholar overseeing its needs, the money goes to him, and adding that the poor of his town and theirs alike rely on him.
megillah-27a-23-25.why: A teaching just cited rules that townspeople who pledge charity while visiting another town take the money home for their own poor; this story shows the exception, when the town has a scholar in charge of its needs.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who decreed the fast and kept the charity, saying the poor of both towns rely on him.

people.name: Rav Hana bar Hanilai
people.about: He came with the people of his town to Rav Huna on the fast day.

terms.meaning: A public fast declared by the community's leaders, often in time of trouble, when people also gave charity.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core text the Gemara discusses.
A Torah scholar responsible for managing a community's affairs, including the use of charity funds.

megillah-27b-20-21.note: Rav Huna once stood before Rav with a piece of straw tied around him for a belt. Rav asked what this was. Rav Huna said he had had no wine to sanctify the Sabbath day, so he pawned his belt and bought wine with it. Rav said: may it be God's will that you be wrapped in silk. Later, at the wedding of Rav Huna's son Rabba, Rav Huna, a short man, was lying on a bed, and his daughters and daughters-in-law came in and threw their silk garments on him until he was wrapped in silk. When Rav heard, he was angry: why, when I blessed you, did you not answer, And likewise to the Master?
megillah-27b-20-21.why: The Gemara is recounting how Sages explained their long lives. Rabbi Zakkai credited his care never to miss sanctifying the Sabbath over wine, even when his mother sold her kerchief to buy it; Rav Huna's sacrifice for the same mitzva, and its reward, follow.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: He pawned his belt to buy wine for the Sabbath blessing and was later covered in silk.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who blessed Rav Huna that he be wrapped in silk.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Rav Huna's son, at whose wedding the blessing came true.

terms.meaning: The blessing over wine said at the start of the Sabbath, known as kiddush.
A customary reply to a blessing, wishing the same good on the one who gave it.

megillah-28a-6-6.note: Rav Huna was walking home with a hoe on his shoulder. Rav Ḥana bar Ḥanilai came and, out of respect for his teacher, took it from him to carry it himself. Rav Huna said: if you are used to carrying such things in your own town, carry it; if not, I do not want to be honored through your degradation.
megillah-28a-6-6.why: Rabbi Neḥunya ben HaKana said he earned long life partly because he never gained honor through another's degradation. The Gemara offers Rav Huna's refusal as an example of what that means.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage carrying his own hoe, who would not let his student carry it for him if that would shame the student.

people.name: Rav Ḥana bar Ḥanilai
people.about: Rav Huna's student, who offered to carry the hoe.

megillah-28a-9-10.note: Rabbi Akiva asked Rabbi Nehunya the Great what virtue had earned him a long life. Rabbi Nehunya's attendants took the question as disrespect and began beating Rabbi Akiva, who climbed to the top of a date palm. From there he asked another question: if the Torah says the daily offering is a lamb, why does it add the word one? Hearing this, Rabbi Nehunya told his attendants that he was a young Torah scholar and to let him be. He answered that one means the finest of the flock, and that his long life came because he never accepted gifts, never insisted on getting even with those who wronged him, and was openhanded with his money.
megillah-28a-9-10.why: The Gemara is explaining each of Rabbi Nehunya's virtues by pointing to the conduct of other Sages, and goes on to similar stories of Sages asked how they merited long life.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The young scholar who asks Rabbi Nehunya about his long life and is beaten by the attendants.

people.name: Rabbi Nehunya the Great
people.about: The aged Sage who stops his attendants and answers Rabbi Akiva.

terms.meaning: The lamb sacrificed in the Temple every morning and every afternoon.

megillah-28b-14-15.note: Reish Lakish was traveling and came to a deep puddle; a man came along, lifted him onto his shoulders and began carrying him across. Reish Lakish asked whether he had read the Bible; he had. Had he studied Mishna? Four of its orders, the man said. Reish Lakish said: you have hewn four mountains and you carry the son of Lakish on your shoulders? Throw the son of Lakish into the water. The man said he was glad to serve the Master. Then, said Reish Lakish, learn from me this teaching of Rabbi Zeira: Jewish women took on themselves to wait seven clean days even for a spot of blood the size of a mustard seed.
megillah-28b-14-15.why: Reish Lakish taught that one who makes use of a person who studies halakha will perish, and Ulla said one may be served by someone who studies four orders of Mishna but not by one who teaches them. The story shows Reish Lakish living by his own rule.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage who refused to be carried by a learned man until he had taught him something.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: The Sage whose saying introduces the story.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: The Sage whose teaching Reish Lakish passed on to the man.

terms.meaning: The early compilation of Jewish law, divided into six orders, or large sections.
The days a woman counts without any sign of blood after her period before immersing in a ritual bath.
Reish Lakish speaking of himself by his family name.

megillah-29a-5-5.note: Abaye said that in Babylonia the Divine Presence rests at times in the ancient synagogue of Huzal and at times in the synagogue that was destroyed and rebuilt in Neharde'a, and that whenever he was within a parasang of one, he went in to pray there. Once the father of Shmuel and Levi were sitting in the Neharde'a synagogue when the Divine Presence came; they heard a loud sound, rose and left. Another time Rav Sheshet was sitting there when the Divine Presence came, and he did not leave. The ministering angels came and frightened him. He said before God: when one is wretched and the other is not, who should give way to whom? God said to the angels: leave him.
megillah-29a-5-5.why: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai has just taught that the Divine Presence went with the Jewish people into every exile, Babylonia included. The Gemara asks where in Babylonia it rests, and these accounts answer.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who named the two synagogues and made a point of praying in them.

people.name: the father of Shmuel
people.about: He left the synagogue when the Divine Presence came.

people.name: Levi
